blocks.text: A railway rail steel contains about 0.7 to 0.8 wt% carbon and is almost entirely pearlite, which is why it resists wear under wheel loads, while the 0.2 wt% carbon steel in a car body is mostly soft ferrite. The iron-carbon diagram predicts this difference from carbon content alone.

blocks.markdown:
The iron-carbon (Fe-Fe$_3$C) phase diagram shows which phases exist at equilibrium for any carbon content and temperature. Only the iron-rich side, up to 6.70 wt% C (the composition of the compound cementite), matters in practice. Three solid phases are important:

- **Ferrite** ($\alpha$): BCC iron with very little carbon, a maximum of about 0.022 wt% C at 727 degrees C. Soft and ductile.
- **Austenite** ($\gamma$): FCC iron that dissolves up to about 2.14 wt% C at 1147 degrees C. Stable at high temperature.
- **Cementite** (Fe$_3$C): an intermetallic compound with 6.70 wt% C. Hard and brittle.

blocks.title: Eutectoid reaction and pearlite
blocks.text: At the eutectoid point, about 0.76 wt% C and 727 degrees C, austenite transforms on cooling into ferrite and cementite: $\gamma\rightarrow\alpha+\mathrm{Fe_3C}$. The product is **pearlite**, a fine lamellar mixture of alternating plates of ferrite and cementite. (Note: these values are the ones used in this course; textbooks quote the eutectoid temperature as 723 or 727 degrees C.)

blocks.caption: Key points of the Fe-Fe$_3$C diagram (typical textbook values).

blocks.markdown: **Steels and cast irons.** Alloys up to about 2.14 wt% C are steels; they can be hot worked in the austenite field. Above this composition the alloy passes through the eutectic reaction and is a cast iron. Steels are subdivided: *hypoeutectoid* below 0.76 wt% C, *eutectoid* at 0.76 wt% C, and *hypereutectoid* between 0.76 and 2.14 wt% C.

**Microstructure of a hypoeutectoid steel.** Cool austenite of composition $C_0$ slowly. In the upper part of the two-phase region (austenite plus ferrite), proeutectoid ferrite forms at the austenite grain boundaries. The carbon rejected by the ferrite enriches the remaining austenite until it reaches 0.76 wt% C at 727 degrees C, where all of it becomes pearlite. The microstructure just below 727 degrees C is therefore proeutectoid ferrite plus pearlite. The lever rule, applied to the tie line at 727 degrees C between 0.022 and 0.76 wt% C, gives the fractions:

blocks.caption: $W_{\alpha'}$: mass fraction of proeutectoid ferrite; $W_p$: mass fraction of pearlite; $C_0$ in wt% C, with $0.022<C_0<0.76$.

blocks.title: Phase and constituent fractions for a 0.45 wt% C steel
blocks.prompt: A steel with 0.45 wt% C is cooled slowly to just below 727 degrees C. Find the fractions of proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite, and the total fractions of ferrite and cementite.

steps.text: The alloy is hypoeutectoid ($0.022<0.45<0.76$). Proeutectoid ferrite fraction by the lever rule.
For the total amounts of the two phases, use the tie line from ferrite (0.022) to cementite (6.70).

blocks.answer: 42.0 percent proeutectoid ferrite and 58.0 percent pearlite; in terms of phases, 93.6 percent ferrite and 6.4 percent cementite, since pearlite contains most of the cementite.

blocks.markdown: **Hypereutectoid steels** behave in the mirror-image way: proeutectoid cementite forms on the austenite grain boundaries until the remaining austenite reaches 0.76 wt% C, which then becomes pearlite. The fractions are $W_{\mathrm{Fe_3C}'}=(C_0-0.76)/(6.70-0.76)$ and $W_p=(6.70-C_0)/(6.70-0.76)$.

blocks.title: Reading the diagram for a hypereutectoid steel
blocks.prompt: A 1.2 wt% C steel is slowly cooled to just below 727 degrees C. Find the fraction of proeutectoid cementite and of pearlite.

steps.text: Check the range: $0.76<1.2<2.14$, so the steel is hypereutectoid.
Proeutectoid cementite: tie line from 0.76 to 6.70 wt% C.

blocks.answer: About 7.4 percent proeutectoid cementite and 92.6 percent pearlite.

items: Carbon content below 0.76 wt%: ferrite plus pearlite; soft and ductile as carbon falls.
At 0.76 wt%: fully pearlitic; stronger and harder.
Above 0.76 wt% up to 2.14: pearlite plus grain-boundary cementite; harder, more brittle.
Above 2.14 wt%: cast irons; low melting temperature and good castability.

blocks.title: Equilibrium only
blocks.text: The diagram describes very slow cooling. Faster cooling shifts temperatures and may produce non-equilibrium microstructures such as bainite or martensite, covered in the heat-treatment module.

points: The eutectoid point is at about 0.76 wt% C and 727 degrees C, where austenite transforms to pearlite (ferrite plus cementite).
For a hypoeutectoid steel, the proeutectoid ferrite fraction is $(0.76-C_0)/(0.76-0.022)$ and the pearlite fraction is $(C_0-0.022)/(0.76-0.022)$.
Steels contain up to about 2.14 wt% C; higher carbon content makes the alloy a cast iron.

questions.stem: Where is the eutectoid point of the Fe-Fe$_3$C system?

options.text: About 0.76 wt% C at 727 degrees C
About 4.30 wt% C at 1147 degrees C
About 0.022 wt% C at 727 degrees C
About 2.14 wt% C at 1147 degrees C

questions.correctOptionText: About 0.76 wt% C at 727 degrees C

distractorRationale.a: Correct: austenite of this composition transforms to pearlite on cooling through 727 degrees C.
distractorRationale.b: This is the eutectic point, where liquid transforms to austenite plus cementite.
distractorRationale.c: This is the maximum solubility of carbon in ferrite, one end of the tie line, not the eutectoid composition.
distractorRationale.d: This is the maximum solubility of carbon in austenite and the nominal steel/cast-iron boundary.

questions.explanation: The eutectoid is the single point on the solid side of the diagram where one solid phase (austenite) transforms on cooling into two others (ferrite and cementite). In the Fe-Fe$_3$C diagram it is at about 0.76 wt% C and 727 degrees C.

questions.stem: An iron-carbon alloy contains 3.2 wt% C. How is it classified?

options.text: Cast iron, because it has more than about 2.14 wt% C
Hypereutectoid steel, because it has more than 0.76 wt% C
Wrought iron, because it is below 4.30 wt% C
Pure iron, because carbon is a minor addition

questions.correctOptionText: Cast iron, because it has more than about 2.14 wt% C

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the steel/cast-iron boundary is the maximum solubility of carbon in austenite, 2.14 wt% C.
distractorRationale.b: Hypereutectoid steels lie between 0.76 and 2.14 wt% C; at 3.2 wt% the alloy contains a eutectic and is a cast iron.
distractorRationale.c: Wrought iron is a nearly carbon-free iron; 4.30 wt% C is the eutectic composition, not a classification boundary for steel.
distractorRationale.d: Pure iron has under about 0.022 wt% C.

questions.explanation: Steels contain up to about 2.14 wt% C, the limit of carbon solubility in austenite, and are worked and heat treated in the solid state. Alloys with more carbon pass through the eutectic reaction on cooling and are cast irons.

questions.stem: Cementite, Fe$_3$C, appears in the iron-carbon diagram. Which description is correct?

options.text: A hard, brittle intermetallic compound with 6.70 wt% C
A soft, ductile solid solution with 0.022 wt% C
A high-temperature FCC solid solution
The liquid phase at 4.30 wt% C

questions.correctOptionText: A hard, brittle intermetallic compound with 6.70 wt% C

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the Fe$_3$C composition is 6.70 wt% C.
distractorRationale.d: The liquid is not cementite; 4.30 wt% C is the eutectic composition.

questions.explanation: Cementite is a compound of fixed stoichiometry: three iron atoms to one carbon atom, which by mass is 6.70 wt% C. It is hard and brittle, and in pearlite it forms thin lamellae alternating with ferrite.

questions.stem: A slowly cooled plain-carbon steel contains 0.20 wt% C. Using the lever rule with a eutectoid composition of 0.76 wt% C and a ferrite solubility of 0.022 wt% C at 727 degrees C, calculate the percentage of pearlite in the microstructure just below 727 degrees C.
questions.explanation: Just below the eutectoid temperature the pearlite is the former eutectoid austenite, so its fraction is $W_p=(C_0-0.022)/(0.76-0.022)=(0.20-0.022)/0.738=0.241$. The remaining 75.9 percent is proeutectoid ferrite that formed above 727 degrees C.

questions.stem: A slowly cooled steel contains 0.35 wt% C. Using a eutectoid composition of 0.76 wt% C and 0.022 wt% C in ferrite, calculate the percentage of proeutectoid ferrite just below 727 degrees C.
questions.explanation: The proeutectoid ferrite fraction is $W_{\alpha'}=(0.76-C_0)/(0.76-0.022)=(0.76-0.35)/0.738=0.556$. This is the lever rule applied to the tie line just above 727 degrees C between ferrite (0.022 wt% C) and austenite (0.76 wt% C), measured from the alloy composition to the austenite end.

questions.stem: A micrograph of a slowly cooled hypoeutectoid steel shows that 50 percent of the area is proeutectoid ferrite (the rest is pearlite). Using 0.76 wt% C for the eutectoid and 0.022 wt% C for ferrite, calculate the carbon content of the steel in wt% C.
questions.explanation: Rearranging $W_{\alpha'}=(0.76-C_0)/(0.76-0.022)$ gives $C_0=0.76-W_{\alpha'}(0.738)=0.76-0.5(0.738)=0.391$ wt% C. This assumes the area fractions equal the mass fractions, which is approximately true because the densities of ferrite and pearlite are similar.

questions.stem: A 1.0 wt% C steel is cooled slowly from 900 degrees C (austenite) to room temperature. What is the room-temperature microstructure and the pearlite fraction? Use 6.70 wt% C for cementite and 0.76 wt% C for the eutectoid.

options.text: Proeutectoid cementite on the grain boundaries plus pearlite, with about 96 percent pearlite
Proeutectoid ferrite plus pearlite, with about 96 percent pearlite
Proeutectoid cementite plus pearlite, with about 4 percent pearlite
All pearlite, with 100 percent pearlite

questions.correctOptionText: Proeutectoid cementite on the grain boundaries plus pearlite, with about 96 percent pearlite

distractorRationale.b: A steel above the eutectoid composition forms proeutectoid cementite, not ferrite.
distractorRationale.c: The fractions have been swapped; the cementite is about 4 percent.
distractorRationale.d: Only the eutectoid composition of 0.76 wt% C is entirely pearlite.

questions.explanation: Hypereutectoid steel first rejects proeutectoid cementite as it cools into the austenite plus cementite field, which lowers the austenite carbon content toward 0.76 wt%. At 727 degrees C the remaining austenite becomes pearlite; the lever rule gives pearlite $=(6.70-1.0)/(6.70-0.76)=0.960$.

questions.stem: An alloy of 4.30 wt% C is heated from room temperature. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is a cast iron whose melting begins and ends at about 1147 degrees C, the lowest melting temperature of any iron-carbon alloy
It is a steel that melts over a wide temperature range
It melts at 1538 degrees C, the melting point of pure iron
It is a hypoeutectoid steel that transforms at 727 degrees C

questions.correctOptionText: It is a cast iron whose melting begins and ends at about 1147 degrees C, the lowest melting temperature of any iron-carbon alloy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the eutectic composition melts at a single temperature, the minimum on the liquidus.
distractorRationale.b: At 4.30 wt% C the alloy is a cast iron, and being at the eutectic composition it melts at one temperature.
distractorRationale.c: 1538 degrees C is the melting point of pure iron, which is higher than any melting in this system.
distractorRationale.d: 727 degrees C is the eutectoid temperature, for compositions near 0.76 wt% C.

questions.explanation: The eutectic composition of 4.30 wt% C is the lowest-melting alloy in the system, with liquid transforming to austenite plus cementite at 1147 degrees C. This low melting point and good castability are why cast irons are used for castings, and the alloy is well above the 2.14 wt% C steel limit.

questions.stem: Describe the equilibrium microstructural changes during slow cooling of a 0.40 wt% C steel from the single-phase austenite field to room temperature. State the phases present and their carbon contents at the main stages and give the final constituents.
markingGuide: Austenite (FCC) single phase at high temperature, with 0.40 wt% C (1 mark)
Cooling below the upper critical (ferrite start) line, proeutectoid ferrite nucleates at austenite grain boundaries (2 marks)
As ferrite grows, the remaining austenite becomes richer in carbon, approaching 0.76 wt% C (2 marks)
At 727 degrees C the remaining austenite (0.76 wt% C) transforms by the eutectoid reaction to pearlite, lamellae of ferrite and cementite (2 marks)
Final microstructure: proeutectoid ferrite plus pearlite (1 mark)
Ferrite contains about 0.022 wt% C at 727 degrees C (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The ferrite rejects carbon into the remaining austenite, enriching it to the eutectoid composition at 727 degrees C, where it becomes pearlite. The result is proeutectoid ferrite plus pearlite, with about 49 percent proeutectoid ferrite and 51 percent pearlite by the lever rule.

questions.stem: A steel has 0.60 wt% C and is slowly cooled to just below 727 degrees C. Calculate the mass fractions of proeutectoid ferrite and pearlite, and the total mass fractions of ferrite and cementite (use 0.022, 0.76 and 6.70 wt% C for ferrite, the eutectoid and cementite).
markingGuide: Explains that most cementite is inside pearlite as lamellae, so cementite total is about 8.7 percent while pearlite is 78 percent (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The two tie lines give different pairs of constituents: the line from 0.022 to 0.76 gives proeutectoid ferrite (0.217) and pearlite (0.783), while the line from 0.022 to 6.70 gives total ferrite (0.913) and cementite (0.087). Pearlite itself is a mixture of ferrite and cementite.
